planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or spring divisions into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil; seed germinates slowly and erratically without cold-moist stratification, so most gardeners start from nursery stock rather than direct seed.

directions: Native to wet mountain grasslands, marsh edges, and seasonally damp meadows of Honshu, Japan, this clump-forming gentian carries whorled, lance-shaped leaves on upright stems that stay evenly moist through the growing season. From late summer into fall it produces an unusually heavy succession of large, upward-facing, deep-blue trumpet flowers clustered in the upper leaf axils, often flowering later and more profusely than the related Gentiana scabra. It is the principal parent behind several garden hybrid gentians bred for border reliability, and it resents soil that dries out even briefly, so site it where moisture never lapses. Divide established clumps only occasionally in spring, since they sulk and need a season to recover from disturbance.

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts into lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; because this species forms tight clumps rather than spreading stolons, it establishes slowly and won't fill in as fast as common Ajuga reptans.

directions: Native to rocky hillsides, open woodland, and scrub of the Italian peninsula, Tenore's bugle forms a tight, non-running rosette clump rather than spreading by the long stolons typical of carpet bugleweed, so it stays put instead of carpeting ground. Short upright spikes of violet-blue flowers appear above the foliage in spring, similar in color to common bugleweed but on a far more restrained plant. Breeders prize it as a parent for taming the aggressive spread of Ajuga reptans while keeping showy flowers and foliage color, as in Chris Hansen's Feathered Friends series of controlled-spread bugle hybrids. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade and divide congested clumps in spring only when needed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into well-drained soil in part sun to full sun; sharp winter drainage matters far more to this sedge's survival than cold air temperatures.

directions: This is the wild New Zealand species behind the widely sold 'Frosty Curls' selection, native to rocky, well-drained slopes and streambanks of the South Island. It forms a dense, cascading, evergreen tussock of very fine, hair-like, pale green to whitish foliage that arches outward and curls gently at the tips, with somewhat less pronounced curling than cultivars selected from it. Inconspicuous brown flower spikes appear against the pale foliage in summer but add little ornamental value of their own. It tolerates full sun to light shade and needs sharp winter drainage more than it needs mild winter temperatures, struggling badly in heavy, waterlogged soil; comb out dead blades by hand each spring and divide crowded clumps to keep new growth coming.
